name: Disposition effect
statement: Investors sell shares that have risen since purchase at a higher rate than shares that have fallen, and the gap survives in tax years where the opposite would pay.
meaning: The claim is about rates, not counts. An investor holding twenty rising stocks and two falling ones will sell more winners than losers whatever their preferences, so the measure has to condition on opportunity. Odean's version divides realised gains by realised plus unrealised gains, and realised losses by realised plus unrealised losses. The two proportions are then compared. A ratio above one says that a position in profit is more likely to be closed on a given day than a position at a loss of the same age. Three claims are often run together under the one name. The first is the trading pattern itself, which is a fact about records. The second is that the pattern costs money, which needs a return comparison. The third is that prospect theory explains it, which is a claim about mechanism and is the weakest of the three.

origin.note: "The Disposition to Sell Winners Too Early and Ride Losers Too Long: Theory and Evidence" supplied the name. Its own contribution is a framework rather than a dataset. The abstract sets out four elements, prospect theory, mental accounting, regret aversion and self-control, and argues that tax considerations alone cannot account for the observed pattern of gain and loss realisation. It also argues that the concentration of loss realisations in December fits the framework and not fully rational behaviour. The measurement that made the claim testable on trading records came thirteen years later, from Odean.

evidence: Odean obtained the 1987 to 1993 trading records of 10,000 accounts at a large discount brokerage. Aggregated over the whole period, the proportion of gains realised was 0.148 and the proportion of losses realised 0.098, a ratio a little over 1.5. The one-tailed test that gains are realised no faster than losses is rejected with a t-statistic above 35. Odean also ran the test at account level rather than trade level, which weakens the independence assumption. Average account PGR was 0.57, average PLR 0.36, and the mean difference of 0.21 gives t = 19. December runs the other way. In December the proportion of losses realised was 0.128 against a proportion of gains realised of 0.108, and from January to November the figures were 0.094 and 0.152. Tax selling appears, and only in the last month. Grinblatt and Keloharju repeated the question on the Finnish Central Securities Depository register, the official daily record of holdings and trades of virtually all Finnish investors from 27 December 1994 to 10 January 1997. Their logit of sell against hold carries 206 regressors, including dummies for each stock, each month and 22 past-return windows. For households, on 122,765 observations, an extreme capital loss of more than 30 percent makes a sale 0.32 less likely than a capital gain at a predicted logit of zero, and a moderate loss 0.21 less likely. The equivalent OLS figures are 0.17 and 0.12.

replication.headline: The pattern reappears in the near-complete register of Finnish share ownership, in a second US brokerage sample and in retail records from several other markets, which is a stronger record than most entries on this site can show.
replication.detail: What distinguishes this case is the kind of repeat available. Most of the corpus is replicated by running an experiment again on fresh volunteers. Here the tests run on the administrative record of what people actually did with their own money, in different countries, under different tax codes, with sample sizes in the tens of thousands and no experimenter present. That removes demand characteristics, hypothetical stakes and small student samples in one move, which is why the pattern itself is close to settled. Grinblatt and Keloharju's Finnish register covers virtually every domestic investor rather than a sample of one broker's clients, and their controls include the stock, the month and the shape of past returns. The raw distributions in the same paper show the effect without controls: the density of realised returns drops sharply just to the left of zero, while the density of paper returns is smooth across zero. Chang, Solomon and Westerfield used 128,829 accounts at a large discount broker from January 1991 to November 1996, comprising 73,558 households, and estimated selling as a regression on a gain dummy. For stocks the coefficient runs from 0.0391 across all investors to 0.0157 among investors who hold both stocks and funds, against a base probability of selling of 21.7 and 18.9 percent. Barber and Odean's review of the field collects the rest and reports the figures the site has not read at source. In their own hazard model on the discount-broker data, a stock up 18 to 22 percent since purchase is 2.65 times more likely to be sold than one within two percent of its purchase price, and 1.77 times more likely than one down 18 to 22 percent. They report Finnish data from 1995 to 2008 with a similar shape. From their survey: Chinese investors in one brokerage were 67 percent more likely to sell a winner than a loser across almost 50,000 accounts, Taiwanese individual investors nearly four times as likely, and US mutual funds realised gains at a rate 21 percent above losses from 1980 to 2002, rising to 72 percent for funds in the previous year's worst-performing quintile. Feng and Seasholes report in their abstract that sophistication and trading experience together remove the reluctance to realise losses while cutting the propensity to realise gains by 37 percent without removing it. Weber and Camerer's laboratory version, as described by Barber and Odean, had subjects sell winners at a 50 percent higher rate than losers, with 60 percent of sales being winners.

study.cite: Grinblatt, M., & Keloharju, M. (2001). What makes investors trade? The Journal of Finance, 56(2), 589-616.

limits: Replication of a pattern is not replication of an explanation, and the two have come apart here. Ben-David and Hirshleifer went back to discount-broker records covering 77,037 accounts from 1990 to 1996 and asked whether selling jumps at exactly zero profit, which is what a preference for realising gains rather than losses predicts. It mostly does not. The probability of selling is V-shaped in profit, rising with the size of a gain and also with the size of a loss, and for positions held 1 to 20 days the discontinuity at zero is never significant and runs from about zero to 0.6 percent of the unconditional probability of selling. Pooled across all holding periods the jump reaches 4.1 to 5.7 percent, which they call economically minor. Barberis and Xiong report that prospect theory preferences defined over annual gains and losses often fail to predict a disposition effect at all, and that a version defined over realised gains and losses predicts it more reliably. None of these studies randomises anything. They compare investors who happen to be sitting on gains with investors sitting on losses, so beliefs, tax position, margin calls and rebalancing are controlled statistically rather than by design. The samples are also not populations. Odean's and Ben-David and Hirshleifer's are the clients of one discount broker, and the Finnish register drops foreign investors, who can register under a nominee, along with any holding whose purchase price falls outside the window. Stephen Cheung's 2025 meta-analysis of experimental disposition-effect studies was located during this check but no readable copy was obtainable at SSRN, the University of Sydney repository or the working-paper host, so none of its figures appear here. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex and the web found no multi-site preregistered replication of the kind this site usually reports, which is unsurprising given that the evidence is archival rather than experimental.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating the effect as a demonstration of loss aversion. It is not the same claim. Loss aversion is a ratio between the weights on gains and losses of equal size, and this site's entry on loss aversion records how unstable that ratio is. The disposition effect is a fact about when positions are closed, and it survives whatever happens to lambda. Gal and Rucker, quoted in that entry, put it in the class of findings that cannot speak to the ratio at all. It is also not the sunk-cost effect. Holding a losing share commits no new money, while the cases in the sunk-cost entry turn on spending more because of what was already spent. A second error is assuming investors are right about the rebound. Odean measured returns after the decision, in excess of the CRSP value-weighted index. Over the following 252 trading days the winners that were sold returned 2.35 percent and the losers that were held minus 1.06 percent, a gap of 3.41 percent with a bootstrapped p-value of 0.001. Over 84 days the gap is 1.03 percent and over 504 days 3.58 percent. A third error is calling the effect universal. Odean's own December figures reverse it. Chang, Solomon and Westerfield found the reverse in the same accounts for delegated assets: the gain coefficient for equity mutual funds runs from minus 0.0656 to minus 0.0485, so investors were 4.85 to 6.56 percent less likely to sell a fund standing at a gain. Whatever produces the pattern in stocks does not travel to money handed to someone else. The last error is reading the strength of the replication record as support for the prospect-theory story that gave the effect its name. The trading pattern is well established. The reason for it is not.
